name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: City, state employees are proud of their work but face burnout, harassment
text:
Justin Hubly, executive director of the Nebraska Association of Public Employees, leads a news conference in December 2023 in Lincoln. New national research found high levels of job satisfaction among public employees, but high levels of burnout and harassment at work. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)State and local government employees report high levels of job satisfaction across the country, but face significant rates of burnout and on-the-job harassment.
That’s according to a new national survey of nearly 5,000 public servants across all 50 states released last week by The People Lab at Harvard University’s Kennedy School. Researchers say the survey, which includes respondents from hundreds of local governments, provides the nation’s most comprehensive analysis of workplace conditions in local governments.
Most employees reported high levels of job satisfaction: 82% said they were at least somewhat satisfied with their job, while 60% said they were satisfied or very satisfied.
Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she is dropping reelection bid 

“That’s good news that people are still kind of proud to say they work for the government,” said Elizabeth Linos, faculty director of The People Lab.
But 40% of employees also reported experiencing at least one symptom of burnout. And 27% said they intended to leave their jobs in the next 12 months.
“You have such a big portion of your public sector workforce that are burnt out on any given day,” Linos said. “…And it’s not the pandemic and it’s not a particular crisis, so to me that says a lot about how much work we have to do to support our public servants.”
State employees consistently reported less favorable workforce conditions than their city and county counterparts, with lower satisfaction, lower engagement and a substantially higher intent to leave.
The study initially aimed to survey local government employees, so it includes results from only about 320 state employees, compared with more than 4,400 employees in city, county and other local governments.
Linos said future analyses would include more state employees to better understand the distinctions between levels of government. She expects the research may mirror polling on public perception of government, which finds people report more faith in their local governments than the federal government.
“You could imagine a world where being able to see the impact of your work more directly leads to more workplace satisfaction than if you have to kind of make the case for how your work has impact, if you work at higher levels of government,” she said.
In the survey, 35% of employees reported experiencing harassment at work over the past year, defined as being bullied, threatened, attacked or harassed. That included 22% who reported harassment from internal sources such as coworkers or supervisors, while 17% reported harassment from external sources such as residents or the media. Those who reported harassment were far more likely to report emotional exhaustion at work and intentions to leave their jobs.
Harassment levels were higher among local government employees and employees who identified as female, non-binary or other gender.
Among those who shared their political party affiliation, Republican and Democratic public servants reported more favorable workforce conditions than independents across nearly every measure.
Linos said the results should inform policymakers and government leaders alike. Every societal challenge — from transportation to climate change to housing — relies on a functioning public sector, she said.
“The people of government, to me, are the central component of that capacity,” she said. “So if we don’t understand and appreciate the work that the people of government do, we’re not going to be able to solve the bigger public policy challenges that we’re trying to solve, and oftentimes that work is hidden from the public.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Crime Statistics dashboard shows 9 convictions for illegal voting in 35 million ballots cast
text:
Early voting in Ohio at the Franklin County Board of Elections. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal) The latest evidence challenging Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose’s repeated demands for more voter fraud prosecutions comes from an unlikely source: fellow Republican Dave Yost, the state’s former attorney general.
The information is found in a new online database — Ohio Crime Statistics Dashboard — that shows for the first time how many of the more than 1,200 cases LaRose referred for investigation since taking office in 2019 have resulted in felony convictions.
The dashboard’s answer: no more than 16 — nine for illegally voting and seven for illegally registering to vote.
If LaRose were a baseball player and convictions were hits as a fraction of his referrals, his batting average would be a minuscule .013.
Baseball doesn’t have enough decimal places to illustrate the vanishingly small share — 0.00003 percent — of the nine convictions for illegal voting among the more than 35 million ballots cast in Ohio in the decade covered by Yost’s dashboard, which was opened to the public in June.
The attorney general’s news release unveiling the dashboard cautions that its data may not be complete because it “relies on self-reported data from hundreds of agencies.” That said, the dashboard is the only tool available to the public that allows statewide counts of convictions for specific crimes.
LaRose, who is barred by term limits from seeking a third term and is running for state auditor in November, acknowledged “voter fraud is rare in Ohio” in a 2021 news release announcing he had referred 117 noncitizens for investigation of suspected election fraud violations. 
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“One of the reasons it’s rare is because we have good laws on the books,” he stated. “These are small numbers, but there is no such thing as an acceptable level of voter fraud.”
Neither LaRose nor his news media staff responded to repeated requests for comment or to detailed written questions.
LaRose isn’t the only Republican in Ohio or the nation to push hard for investigations of voter fraud.
President Donald Trump has claimed repeatedly that the 2020 election was “stolen” through widespread fraud and that “millions of people who voted illegally” cost him the popular vote in 2016.
A decade earlier, President George W. Bush’s administration fired nine U.S. attorneys, at least two of whom had declined to bring voter fraud cases for lack of evidence. A Justice Department inspector general later found “substantial evidence” that some firings were partisan. 
Critics argue that Republicans fan fears of widespread voter fraud to justify tighter regulations governing elections — such as photo ID, documentary proof of citizenship and limits on mail-in ballots — that make voting harder for lower-income voters, who historically have tended to vote Democratic.
Over the last two decades Ohio has generally raised the bar to vote. 

In 2006, the same year Ohio allowed no-excuse absentee voting by mail or in person for the first time, voters were required to show identification, although utility bills and other documents were accepted.
In 2014, three years after a referendum drive forced repeal of a law that sharply cut early voting, the legislature reduced early voting from 35 to 28 days and eliminated “Golden Week,” when people could register and vote at the same time.
In 2023, a law took effect that required most in-person voters to show photo ID, shortened the “grace period” for accepting absentee ballots postmarked before Election Day but received afterward from 10 days to four, ended early voting on the day before Election Day and moved up the deadline to request an absentee ballot.
This year a new law eliminates the “grace period” entirely. 

While some political experts question whether Republicans benefit from lower voter turnout, some conservative strategists have long argued that they do.
“I don’t want everybody to vote,” Paul Weyrich, a founder of the Heritage Foundation, told conservative religious leaders in 1980. “Our leverage in the elections quite candidly goes up as the voting populace goes down.”
LaRose backed his zero-tolerance rhetoric with a steady stream of suspected voter fraud referrals — especially involving noncitizens — to county and state law enforcement officials, but while the number of referrals climbed, few resulted in charges.
A 2023 Ohio Capital Journal investigation found that of 641 referrals, only 18 — less than 3% — resulted in charges. Of those, 13 resulted in convictions, including several that were pleaded down to misdemeanors.
Ohio Sec. of State LaRose has flagged 641 cases of voter fraud. Less than 3% resulted in charges

Those numbers overstate the results of LaRose’s referrals, according to the Capital Journal, which contacted the 60 counties where referrals were sent and received 55 responses. A handful of the cases “likely didn’t come from LaRose’s efforts,” including several that “stem from violations between 2014 and 2016, well before LaRose took office.”
Only one of those convictions involved a noncitizen voting: a Geauga County man, adopted from the Caribbean as a child, who admitted he knew he couldn’t legally vote but cast ballots from 2014 to 2016.
The county prosecutor said the man — then 60 years old — pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor after “federal officials had suggested they’d deport” him if he was convicted of a felony. The prosecutor said another mitigating factor was that he had checked the “noncitizen” box when registering to vote. The man was sentenced to 10 days in jail.
The Capital Journal noted it was “exceptionally difficult” to follow up on the referrals because LaRose’s office doesn’t track outcomes of cases passed on to the state Bureau of Criminal Investigation or directly to county prosecutors.
Several prosecutors surveyed for the report complained that many of LaRose’s 641 referrals were examples of “mistakes or confusion — incidents like an elderly voter casting a ballot in the wrong precinct.”
One explanation for so few convictions is that many county prosecutors — Republicans and Democrats — don’t pursue cases where people make honest mistakes and do not intend to commit a crime, according to a 2014 survey by the Northeast Ohio Media Group, which was renamed Advance Ohio in 2017 and operates Cleveland.com.
“Prosecutors in counties large and small told the media outlet their investigations typically concluded that the irregularities resulted from confusion by voters or mistakes by election officials rather than from people trying to game the system,” the report stated.
Jon Husted, Ohio’s secretary of state from 2011 to 2019 and now a U.S. senator, had directed all 88 county boards to investigate fraud claims from the 2012 presidential election. The media outlet examined eight counties that had investigated at least 10 reports each; fewer than two dozen charges resulted, and Medina was one of five with none.
Dean Holman, a Democrat and the county’s prosecutor at the time of the survey, cited the case of an elderly woman who returned an absentee ballot, requested a second ballot and tried to vote on Election Day. Investigators concluded that the woman, who was dealing with the death of her husband, did not intend to commit a crime.
“Some of these people were just confused,” he said. “Those people should not be prosecuted. The criminal justice system is designed for criminal conduct.”
In an interview this week, Holman said the vast majority of illegal voting referrals he received during his 28 years as Medina County’s prosecutor “did not result in prosecutions.”
“I can’t recall every case, but I think 90 percent of the cases that were given to me to review were without merit,” he said. “And a prosecutor is ethically bound not to prosecute a case he thinks will not be won at trial.”

The 2014 report told a similar story from Ron O’Brien, a Republican who served 24 years as Franklin County’s prosecutor before losing a reelection bid in 2020.
O’Brien said “16 cases likely will be prosecuted after some further investigation.” But he added that more than 30 cases were dismissed, including “a number of elderly voters who had apparent memory issues, and while they had voted twice or attempted to vote twice, a criminal prosecution was not deemed proper.”
Most of the cases were referrals from county boards of elections, which traditionally were allowed to police their own elections. That began to change in 2016 when legislation sponsored by LaRose when he was a state senator went into effect requiring the secretary of state to check the statewide voter rolls each year for noncitizens.
In August 2024, LaRose re-referred nearly 600 cases of suspected noncitizen registration or voting, which county prosecutors had not pursued, directly to the Ohio attorney general.
“Unfortunately, many of these referrals have not been pursued by law enforcement, sometimes by choice and other times due to limited prosecutorial capacity,” LaRose stated in a news release. 
“State law gives the attorney general the authority to take up these referrals if the prosecuting attorney doesn’t prosecute the violations within a reasonable time.”
LaRose complained that only a dozen of the hundreds of referrals he had made to county prosecutors over the years resulted in charges.
LaRose’s action triggered immediate pushback from Lou Tobin, executive director of the Ohio Prosecuting Attorneys Association.
“We take exception to the idea that prosecutors are not doing their job,” Tobin told the public broadcasting network’s Statehouse News Bureau. “I think the secretary of state just doesn’t like the outcome of our review and so now he is forum shopping by taking these cases to the attorney general.
“These are referrals that often lack minimal evidence necessary to pursue charges or pursue an indictment, let alone obtain a conviction.”
LaRose responded that his job wasn’t to build cases.
“What the law says is that we should report violations,” LaRose told the Statehouse News Bureau. “It doesn’t say that we’re the police department that gathers the evidence.”
In sending the cases to Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost, LaRose said, “I have full confidence that our excellent attorney general takes this seriously and is going to dig into this.”
Yost moved quickly on the referrals, obtaining indictments by mid-October — just a few weeks before the 2024 presidential election — against six noncitizens accused of illegally voting.
But at an Oct. 22 news conference announcing the indictments, Yost voiced frustration with LaRose for referring so many cases in which the only alleged offense involved registering to vote.
Of the nearly 600 referrals, 138 involved actual voting, according to LaRose’s Aug. 21, 2024, news release.
“I need to have a sit down with the secretary of state about the value of those cases where there was no voting — I think that we ought to be focusing on the voting,” Yost said at the news conference. “I don’t really want to pull people off of officer-involved critical incident investigations, child rapists, murderers to be chasing voter registration cases for past elections.”
Illegal voting is a fourth-degree felony in Ohio punishable by up to 18 months in prison. Registering to vote illegally is a fifth-degree felony carrying a maximum sentence of 12 months in prison.
So how have the prosecutions of six noncitizens fared? Nearly two years after the six indictments were filed, there has been a single conviction — and that one is being appealed.

The indictment against Ramesh Patel, 68, of North Royalton, was dropped on Oct. 28, 2024 — 11 days after it was issued — when Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Michael O’Malley pointed out that Patel had died in 2022.
The case against Ahmed Aden, 35 at the time he was indicted, of Columbus, was dismissed on July 17, 2026. Aden, a legal permanent resident but not a citizen, had been accused of voting in 2008 and 2020. In dismissing the case, Franklin County Common Pleas Judge Sheryl Munson ruled that the two-year gap between the closing of the investigation in 2022 and the indictment crippled Aden’s defense. By then he had moved and lost access to the witnesses and documents. The attorney general has appealed the dismissal to the 10th District Court of Appeals.
Maria Dearaujo, then 62, of Columbus, was acquitted May 19, 2026. Franklin County Common Pleas Judge Chris Brown ruled from the bench that she had proven an entrapment defense. The 2005 voter registration form she received at the Bureau of Motor Vehicles had “YES” circled on the citizenship question, according to an Associated Press story. She testified she didn’t circle it. She also testified that in 2015 a BMV clerk told her she could vote. Under Ohio law, the state cannot appeal an acquittal, and double jeopardy bars a retrial.
A 78-year-old Hudson woman who came to the U.S. from Canada as a 12-year-old was indicted on two counts of illegal voting and entered a guilty plea after being booked, fingerprinted and photographed at the Summit County Jail, according to a Signal Cleveland story. But Summit County Common Pleas Judge Kelly McLaughlin ruled in April 2025 that she could enter an intervention in lieu of conviction program, which allows the charges to eventually be dismissed. The case no longer appears in court records, apparently because it was sealed.
The case against Van Thuy Cooper, 53, of Hilliard in Franklin County, is ongoing. According to news reports, she was brought to the United States in the 1970s from Vietnam by her parents. She said in court filings she believed she became naturalized when her mother did. She registered to vote in 2016. In 2020 she received notice from the secretary of state telling her she was not legally permitted to register or vote and directing her to cancel her voter registration, which she did. Local and state officials had investigated her case in 2022 but declined to bring charges. 
The only conviction so far came against Nicholas Fontaine, 32, of Kent, who came from Canada as a toddler.

Fontaine told the Associated Press in 2024 that he registered to vote while in college after registering for the draft, which permanent residents are required to do. He mistakenly assumed he could vote until a Department of Homeland Security official came to his home in 2018 or 2019 — during Trump’s first term — and told him his votes in 2016 and 2018 were illegal. He was warned not to vote again and never did.
He assumed that settled the issue and said he was shocked to be indicted so many years later. He pleaded no contest in May and was placed on probation for 12 months and fined $500 and court costs.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He has appealed his conviction to the 11th District Court of Appeals, arguing that the trial judge erred in not dismissing the case because the state failed to bring charges within the six-year statute of limitations. His no-contest plea, unlike a guilty plea, preserved his right to appeal the judge’s refusal to dismiss the case.
Yost declined to be interviewed for this story, according to a spokesperson for Alliance Defending Freedom, a Christian legal advocacy nonprofit based in Arizona. Yost became the Alliance’s senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation after leaving office on June 7 this year — two days after unveiling the Ohio Crime Statistics Dashboard.
The lack of convictions hasn’t deterred LaRose from continuing to push for more prosecutions. Last October he referred 1,084 cases involving noncitizens to the U.S. Department of Justice.
In appealing to Washington, LaRose acknowledged that many of the cases had been earlier referred to county and state officials who declined to prosecute.
“I have made numerous criminal referrals throughout my administration, with much of the evidence related to unlawful registration and voting activity,” he wrote to the Department’s Criminal Division.
“These cases have encountered varying degrees of adjudication from Ohio’s 88 county prosecutors,” he added. “We now have an executive administration at the White House and the Department of Justice that has expressed an interest in actively reviewing and potentially prosecuting evidence of federal election crimes.”
But in the year since referring the cases to the DOJ, charges have been filed against only three Ohioans, all legal permanent residents:

Cary Ann Patterson, 59, a British citizen, was charged in a criminal complaint with illegally voting in the November 2024 federal election. Records from the Gallia County Board of Elections indicate she falsely registered as a U.S. citizen in 2005 and voted in at least 10 elections, according to a news release from the U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of Ohio.
Arshed Zuberi, 69, a Pakistani citizen, was charged after allegedly registering to vote in 2015 and 2016 by signing a declaration claiming U.S. citizenship. Records from the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections show he voted in at least six elections, according to a news release from the U.S. Attorney of the Northern District of Ohio.
Eliza M. Moss, 63, a citizen of the Philippines, was charged with illegally registering to vote in 2004 and 2023 and voting in several primary and general elections. Ashtabula County records show Moss stated that the person who helped her register told her she could vote despite not being a citizen, according to the Northern District news release.

The Ohio charges, announced Oct. 6, are part of a high-profile flurry of arrests in the weeks leading up to next month’s midterm elections.
“In the last five weeks alone, the department has charged 64 aliens, legal and illegal, across 17 states with unlawful voting and registration offenses,” Kiersten Pels, a Justice Department spokesperson in Washington, D.C., stated in an Oct. 7 email. “Since the beginning of the Trump Administration, DOJ has charged 104 people with voting fraud-related offenses.”
Pels said she didn’t know if any of the three Ohioans charged were among the 1,084 cases LaRose sent to the Department of Justice last year.
In a news release issued hours after the arrests were announced, LaRose stated: “I’m grateful to see justice finally being pursued in these cases, thanks to the unprecedented collaboration between my office and the federal government.”
LaRose’s office did not respond to written questions asking whether the three were among his 2025 referrals and, if not, what other “collaboration” his statement referred to, such as the voter registration data his office provided to the Justice Department in February.
David Knox is an independent journalist, former reporter at the Akron Beacon Journal and former managing editor of The (Medina County) Gazette. He can be reached at dknox@paladinreports.com.
Doug Oplinger, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist and former reporter and editor at the Akron Beacon Journal, contributed to this report. He can be reached at oplingerdoug@gmail.com.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Haitians and their supporters march on Columbus with demands
text:
Haitian immigrants and their supporters on a protest march out of Springfield, Ohio.
(Photo by Marty Schladen, Ohio Capital Journal.)SPRINGFIELD — It’s been a golden autumn week in Ohio as many celebrated some of its happy traditions.
In Circleville, the 119th Pumpkin Show opened this past Wednesday. And in nearby Deer Creek State Park, people readied for the annual Halloween Campout, decorating campsites with fake skeletons, ghouls, graves and other spooky stuff.
But not far away in Springfield, a group of about 40 marched out of town at dawn on a misty Wednesday morning to draw attention to the real nightmare they’re living and to demand action to ease it.
Ohio Haitian immigrants and their supporters embarked on a four-day pilgrimage to Columbus last week with a list of demands related to what they’ve been through since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term.
As many as 15,000 Haitian immigrants were living in Springfield, many with temporary protected status, until Trump and the conservatives on the U.S. Supreme Court ended it in late July. That means they were here legally, and had established new lives after an earthquake devastated their already-shaky home country in 2010.
Conditions in Haiti have only deteriorated since, and the government has almost ceased to function. Gangs are using murder, kidnapping and child rape to project their power ever further.
Some from Springfield have already been rounded up, imprisoned and deported back to what Gov. Mike DeWine called “hell.”
That treatment has come to people who committed no crime, Pastor Reginald Silencieux of the First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield said through an interpreter.
“We’ve had some people who lost their TPS and some of them have been deported and the League of Haitian Pastors are heartbroken by that,” Silencieux said.  “People should not be treated that way. These are good people and humane people.”
Minister Archange Antoine, left, and Pastor Reginald Silencieux. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
Silencieux said he’d been in communication with some of his congregants since their forced return to Haiti.
“It’s a tragedy,” he said. “Can you imagine? You come to Springfield. You work to build the economy. You grow your family. You do everything right, and they just snatch everything away from you. They take away your house. They take away all your belongings. Now (I’m) witnessing their suffering in Haiti. They’re not able to make it. It’s a catastrophe.”
The influx of Haitians to Springfield helped revive a shrinking city and its economy as they filled jobs in warehouses and other places that native-born residents didn’t want. 
With their loss, Springfield now leads the state in year-over-year job losses. Federal job reports show the city’s labor force lost 1,100 manufacturing, leisure and hospitality jobs, contracting 2.2% in 2025 alone.
Now, the International Rescue Committee reports, Springfield’s Haitians are forced to return to a place where not only can’t they find jobs, they’re adding to a humanitarian crisis in a country where half the population lives in acute hunger.
As they undertook the first leg of a four-day journey to Columbus, the Haitians and their supporters were demanding more than just a reinstatement of protected status, which was taken away on a controversial legal basis.
A pilgrimage in support of Springfield, Ohio’s Haitians heads out of town. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
Silencieux said the abuse of Haitians who had protected status starts well before deportation.
Some have been arrested by masked Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and locked up in private, for-profit prisons or county jails run by sheriffs seeking federal money to pad their budgets. Others were summoned to ICE offices to be fitted with ankle monitors.
Silencieux said the former is breaking up families and the latter is a deep insult to descendants of slaves.
“This system of prisons in America, we’re not used to that,” he said. “And the ankle monitors (are) dehumanizing. It’s made us feel that we’re less than human. It makes us remember that these are the same shackles that were used in the time of slavery.”
Wearing an ankle monitor was so humiliating to Pierre Damas Bel — a 20-year-old Wright State University student who was bullied for wearing one — that he took his own life on Aug. 31.
It’s understandable that aside from organizers and clergy, few Haitian immigrants still in Springfield participated in the march. They’re afraid to go out in public, organizers said.
Among the changes the marchers are demanding, they want the ankle monitoring program officially ended, imprisoned Haitians returned to their families and ICE agents out of Springfield.
Even before his second presidency started, Trump was victimizing Springfield’s Haitians. 
In a Sept. 15, 2024 debate, he repeated the false, racist claim that the city’s Haitians were stealing their neighbors’ pets and eating them. Then, with bomb threats shutting down Springfield schools and civic buildings, then-Sen. JD Vance repeated them, doubling down on the threat to his own constituents.
Michaelle Louis had an obviously sunny demeanor as she led songs on the Springfield City Hall Plaza just after dawn Wednesday. But ask about what’s happened to her and her neighbors and a deep anger becomes apparent.
Michaelle Louis, an organizer of Springfield. Ohio’s Haitian community. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)
She declined to say whether she held protected status or whether she faces deportation. 
Louis said she came to the U.S. in 2014 after her brother was assassinated in Port-au-Prince, the Haitian capital, and moved to Springfield in 2021.
She won’t discuss what’s happening to Haitians in the U.S. in terms of immigration status.
“If you’re not born here, you’re faced with deportation,” Louis said. “They don’t care about your citizenship, they don’t care. There have been so many citizens who weren’t born here who have been in detention. It’s not about your status. It’s about what you look like. Are you are Black? This is why I don’t want to talk about immigration. It’s about skin color.”
Perhaps bolstering her point is the fact that amid his mass deportations and restrictions on refugees, Trump in May said he would admit an additional 10,000 white South African refugees this year. They or their ancestors were the architects of the apartheid policy that allowed a tiny white minority rule over the Black majority there until its end in 1994.
The clear racial overtones and the harshness of Trump’s crackdown appear to be backfiring politically, Minister Archange Antoine said as he marched along an overpass leading out of Springfield. Polling has shown that voters have turned against Trump on immigration and staunchly support a path to citizenship for immigrants.
“I definitely think it’s that people are witnessing families being separated,” Antoine said. “They’re seeing citizens being detained. They’re seeing citizens killed. They’re seeing that children are being left alone, hanging. And the question is, ‘Am I responsible for this?'”
The march will culminate in a closing rally in Columbus at 1 p.m. Saturday. It will be held at West Bank Park, 303 W. Main St.

title: Ohio Supreme Court: Village with data center moratorium won’t have to consider site plan
text:
Muncy Township, Lycoming County, is the site of a proposed data center. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)An Ohio village won’t have to consider the proposal from a new data center after putting a moratorium in place, according to a unanimous ruling by the Ohio Supreme Court.
The unanimous decision released this week by the state’s highest court said that the village of Lordstown’s leaders were allowed to stop the process of a data center site-plan review. They were not required to review the plans because, at the time, the village council had banned data centers in their area.
The company attempting to start the site-review, Bristolville 25 Developer, started the process in October of 2025, two weeks before the village council adopted a data center ban. The company had purchased property zoned for industrial use in Lordstown in February of that year, with the specific intent to build a data center.
The day after the site-review was requested in October, the village’s planning and zoning administrator, Kellie Bordner, sent an email to the company notifying them that a ban on data centers had received a second reading before the village council, and that the planning and zoning office “would not be able to proceed until council makes a decision on the ban at the next council meeting,” according to court documents.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.In early November, the council passed a prohibition on data centers in Lordstown, adding that “no zoning permit, building permit, or certificate of occupancy shall be issued for any use that meets the (ordinance’s) definition of a data center.”
But the ban didn’t apply to every data center.
“The ordinance was explicitly inapplicable to any data-center facility already existing or under construction as of the ordinance’s effective date,” the supreme court wrote in their decision.
Still, Bordner and Village Solicitor Matthew Ries said they were working to review the drafts from Bristolville, but Ries predicted the project would “likely be prohibited” by of the new data center ban.
After the supreme court had received the case but before it made any decisions, the village council repealed the data center ban, instead passing an ordinance that would place a “temporary moratorium on the issuing of any new permits, as well as the receipt and processing of applications for permits, for proposed data centers in Lordstown,” supreme court documents stated.
In June, the village also passed a 180-day extension to the moratorium, one of more than 100 data center moratoriums across the state.
The data center developers asked the state supreme court to order that the village follow the review process as it would have done before the moratorium was put in place, arguing that their review was initiated before zoning laws were changed to prohibit the facilities.
The court disagreed, saying the company did not prove the right to have the review based on an out-of-date zoning ordinance. The court further said Bristolville “has not met the legislative requirements for obtaining a permit and therefore has no vested right to enforcement of any particular zoning ordinance.”
“Under the moratorium, the village is under no legal duty to proceed with a site-plan review of Bristolville’s project under (the ordinance) and (the company) has not shown a clear legal right to have Bristolville’s site plan reviewed under the premoratorium zoning ordinance,” the court stated.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ohio incumbent US Sen. Jon Husted’s campaign is trying to portray Sherrod Brown as the incumbent
authors: David J. Jackson, Ph.D., Dominic D. Wells, Ph.D.
text:
Former U.S. Senator Sherrod Brown, left, will take on U.S. Senator Jon Husted, right, in 2026. (Photos by CSPAN/Morgan Trau)There are some peculiar dynamics at play in Ohio’s race for U.S. Senate between Republican incumbent Jon Husted and his Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown.   
What’s a Senator who is running for reelection in a state his party has controlled for most of close to four decades to do when voters think the state and country are going in the wrong direction? Use AI. No, this is not another think piece about Artificial Intelligence.  We mean Artificial Incumbency. Here is what we mean by that.
In 2024 in Ohio longtime Democratic US Senator Sherrod Brown lost a tough re-election fight to Republican Bernie Moreno.  Meanwhile, Ohio’s other Senator, Republican JD Vance won the Vice Presidency. Gov. Mike DeWine appointed his Lieutenant Governor Jon Husted to the Senate seat Vance vacated, and now Brown is running again in a special election to serve out the remainder of the term until 2028.
Since 1992, Ohio Republicans have had a gubernatorial and legislative trifecta for all but seven years. And according to the latest BGSU Poll, likely voters are not happy about the direction of the state of Ohio, with 52% saying the state is off on the wrong track. Additionally, 61% think the same thing about the country as a whole. This is not friendly terrain for an incumbent.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
According to the New York Times, “One Republican strategist in Ohio, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race, said the (Husted) campaign was intentionally casting Mr. Brown as the incumbent, a rare opportunity amid dismal Republican approval ratings for the party to harness anger at the status quo.”  
Husted supporting ads even refer to Brown as “Senator Sherrod Brown.”  
This is what we call Artificial Incumbency: the deliberate attempt to cast your opponent as the currently serving senator when in fact you are the incumbent.
Traditionally, incumbents enjoy a significant advantage over challengers, so one could think this casting of Brown as the incumbent would be to his benefit. However, voter dissatisfaction may be so great that they just want a change.  
In recent years, a populist message has gained traction among voters on the left and right of the political spectrum. Democrats have focused on messages about elite billionaires, which according to the BGSU poll only 14% of voters view favorably.  
Republicans have focused their populist message on political elites, and the same poll shows that only 31% view Democrats in Congress favorably and only 34% view Republicans in Congress favorably. There may be less advantage to being the incumbent in a political climate that is anti-elite.  
Is Husted’s Artificial Incumbency pointed at Brown working? The most recent BGSU Poll shows that 25% of likely voters think Brown is the incumbent. Who are these voters and for which candidate are they likely to vote?
Education appears to be a dominant factor in explaining which likely voters believe Brown is the incumbent, with those with more education generally being more likely to know that Husted is the current Senator. Interestingly, party identification tells us nothing.
Black and women likely voters are more likely than others to believe Brown is the incumbent, while members of union households are less likely to believe Brown is currently serving.
Who do likely voters who think Brown is the incumbent support? While 48.6% of voters overall say they plan to vote for Sherrod Brown, only 44.5% of voters who think Sherrod Brown is the incumbent say they plan to vote for him, while 43.3% say they plan to vote for Husted.  
Interestingly, those who think Brown is the incumbent are more likely than other voters to say they plan to support the Libertarian, independent, or some other candidate, although these percentages are quite small. Could they matter if voters actually stick with these choices and the election is incredibly close? It’s possible.
Ohio Republicans have a problem in that voters are not happy with the direction of the state that Republicans have controlled politically for most of close to 40 years. 
It appears that incumbent U.S.Sen. Jon Husted has utilized the strategy of Artificial Incumbency to create the appearance that former Sen. Sherrod Brown is still in office.  
About a quarter of likely voters believe it and are slightly less likely to vote for Brown because of it. We won’t know until all the votes are counted if the strategy worked.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Ramaswamy ad in Ohio governor campaign has side-effect of highlighting adversity Acton overcame
text:
Ohio Democratic governor candidate and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Dr. Amy Acton, looks on during a rally on April 28, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images.)One side effect of the attack ad being promoted by Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy is that it’s now bringing attention to the inspirational American success story embodied by his opponent Dr. Amy Acton and the adversity she overcame.
By now, nearly everyone in the country has seen or heard about the Ramaswamy campaign ad that platforms Acton’s estranged mother calling her daughter a liar. Nearly everyone also now knows the sad and shocking story behind the ad. 
According to court records, Acton’s stepfather was indicted for raping her during her pre-teen years, allegations that Acton has talked about publicly in the past and that her younger brother, Phil Stearns, corroborated in a public statement on Oct. 20. Acton and Stearns both say they suffered other forms of abuse, hunger and neglect at the hands of Acton’s mother and stepfather during their childhood. 
At the time of the indictment of Acton’s stepfather, Acton and her brother were removed from the home, while her mother — the woman featured in Ramaswamy’s campaign ad — stuck with Acton’s stepfather when he fled Ohio to escape those criminal charges in the late 1970s. He died in Pennsylvania in 2004. Acton says she hasn’t seen or talked to her mother in nearly 50 years.
Rightly so, the Ramaswamy ad has received intense condemnation even from many Republicans, including Dr. Acton’s former boss, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine. In the two or three days after the story broke last week, one couldn’t watch or read the news, or scroll through social media or YouTube, without seeing this story on multiple platforms, often with panels of politicians and media figures representing a wide range of political outlooks all having the same reaction: That Ramaswamy using Acton’s long-estranged mother to discredit her rape survivor daughter was the most despicable, sickest campaign ad they had ever seen.
One thing that the ad, in a backwards way, has put more of a spotlight on is how Amy Acton survived and transcended her abuse and mistreatment as a young girl, eventually graduating at the top of her high school class, working her way through college, and earning a medical degree and master’s in public health. She rose to the top echelons of Ohio state government, leading the Ohio Department of Health steadily and effectively during Ohio’s early response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
She has been the recipient of multiple prestigious honors and awards, including the Columbus Foundation’s Spirit of Columbus Award in 2020, the John F. Kennedy Library Foundation’s Profile in COVID Courage Award in 2021 and the USA Today Woman of the Year for Ohio in 2022, among others. And as of Friday, Acton was the favored candidate for winning the governor’s race in both polling and prediction markets. Until last week, Ohio was considered a decidedly “red” state.
Acton’s perseverance and courage in rising so far above her tragic childhood is the epitome of the inspirational American success story. And the supreme irony? The nearly universal backlash against that rancid campaign ad (with the execrable exceptions of President Trump and Vice President Vance) may help put Dr. Acton over the top with Ohio’s voters on Nov. 3. 
In fact, it’s in the running for the most effective political ad of this mid-term election year, just not in the way that Vivek Ramaswamy had hoped.

A mysterious group that has spent at least $2 million boosting a little-known socialist candidate in Ohio’s highly competitive Senate race is being funded by Republicans, according to a new campaign finance filing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Marching to oppose a new gas pipeline in CT
text:
On Sunday, November 7, at 1 p.m. I will march with fellow protestors] against a new proposed Eversource methane gas pipeline.
We will march from Hurd State Park in East Hampton, which would be impacted by the proposed pipeline, to the Eversource center in that town.
With this march, which will span seven miles and feature speakers and protesters from various groups throughout Connecticut, we hope to raise public awareness of this redundant pipeline that has been proposed and advanced without resident knowledge or support.
Concerned residents and local students as well as clean air and energy advocates submitted concerns to the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) when this pipeline was quietly proposed in early 2025, but there has been little public information since then. In addition to the scoping meeting and comment period, DEEP is conducting an Environmental Impact Evaluation, which has yet to be released.
Connecticut residents have come together against this proposed pipeline due to concerns for the physical environment it will cut through, the cost it will pass on to ratepayers, as well as the long-term climate impact of further methane reliance and the potential reasons for this expansion.
If built, the section of the Eversource Southeast Resilience Project (SERP) being protested will run under the Connecticut River and cut through several state parks. The proposed line would cut under the Connecticut Valley Railroad State Park Trail in Middletown, as well as the Hurd and George Seymour State Parks and Higganum Meadows Wildlife Management Area in Haddam and East Hampton.
The pipeline will be installed via horizontal directional drilling. When this same method was used under the Sakonnet River in Rhode Island, 50 gallons of toxic drilling fluid were spilled into the river, which is incredibly difficult to remove. There are critically important ecosystems and species both in the state parks and the river, and I am deeply concerned that they would be negatively impacted by this expansion.
Further, the cost of pipeline expansions are passed on to ratepayers; the primary way that utilities make money is through investing in big infrastructure upgrades and expansions and then receiving a return on those investments from ratepayers. A recent analysis found that gas customers in Connecticut pay more for pipes than they do for actual gas, and that the amount spent on pipes has significantly increased over the past 25 years. More gas expansion will only raise our rates further.
Finally, we have to question why Eversource wishes to expand their already strong gas pipeline network in Connecticut. There is no need and no demand from ratepayers for more fracked gas pipelines in Connecticut. Our state is awash in so much methane gas that we export 40 percent of power generated here to other states, to the enormous profit of energy companies. Since there is no outstanding need for redundant pipelines such as SERP, I am concerned that it may be constructed in anticipation of AI data centers, which bring their own slew of negative impacts on residents.
I have lived in Connecticut for nearly all my life. I am 23, and have always cared deeply about the environment, this state and its people. As a young person, I am certainly concerned about the state of the environment being left for current and future generations.
Methane gas is a much more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide and building a new pipeline for it worries me greatly. But my concern does not stem purely from a desire to preserve the environment and protect against climate change. The people of Connecticut deserve better. We have been sold a lie that natural gas is the cheapest, safest option for us, and our state has been locked into a reliance on this volatile gas to heat our homes and power our electricity. The only reason “natural” gas is framed as cheaper is because we ratepayers have already paid the bill on putting miles and miles of pipeline in the ground.
But here’s the catch: we will just have to keep on paying for it. And not just for the upkeep or expansion of this infrastructure, but we will also pay with our health.
If you share my concerns, I urge and invite you to walk with me on Sunday, November 7, at 1 p.m. And if you are a decision maker in Connecticut, I ask you to use your voice to stop the SERP pipeline and those like it.
Nick Hopkins lives in Enfield.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Independent US Senate candidate in South Dakota backed by Forward Party
text:
Christine Todd Whitman, former Republican governor of New Jersey and the EPA administrator under President George W. Bush, left, participates in an Oct. 25, 2026, forum in Sioux Falls with Brian Bengs, independent U.S. Senate candidate in South Dakota. Whitman is the co-founder of the Forward Party, which endorsed Bengs. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight)SIOUX FALLS — South Dakota’s independent U.S. Senate candidate, Brian Bengs, said Sunday he “would probably not be here in a competitive position today” without the support he’s gotten from a new political party co-founded by a former Democrat and a former Republican.
Bengs appeared alongside the Forward Party’s CEO and one of those co-founders at a forum attended by around 60 people at Monick Yards, just east of downtown Sioux Falls. Bengs faces Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds in a race with no Democrat on the Nov. 3 ballot.
Christine Todd Whitman, the former Republican governor of New Jersey and EPA administrator during the George W. Bush administration, told the crowd she helped launch the party in 2022 because she feels the current two-party system is broken.
Challenger takes aim at incumbent’s campaign finances in South Dakota US Senate race

After leaving the Bush administration, Whitman wrote the 2005 book “It’s My Party Too,” which criticized Republican moves toward social issues for boxing too many people out of the party. That “was dangerous for the country,” Whitman said on Sunday. She eventually became a registered independent. She came to believe, she said, that major parties have no incentive to turn their focus away from party loyalty and back toward working together to address the country’s problems. 
At this point, Whitman said, “I think our democracy is holding on by a thread, and I’m not about to see it go without putting up a fight.”
She co-founded the Forward Party with Andrew Yang, a former Democrat who ran to be that party’s presidential nominee in 2020 with a campaign that trumpeted his proposal for a “universal basic income” of $1,000 a month for every U.S. adult. The following year, he ran unsuccessfully to be mayor of New York City.
Yang was supposed to be at the forum, but his flight was delayed. Bengs and Whitman invited attendees to a social gathering with them and Yang at Monks Ale House, about a block from Monick Yards.
Bengs: Says Democratic run was about practicality
Bengs told the audience that the first time he ran for Senate in South Dakota, four years ago against Republican Sen. John Thune, Bengs switched his registration from independent to Democrat so he could get the party’s support. 
Parties have built-in communications networks, donor lists and a host of other advantages for candidates. Bengs said he switched so he could access those advantages, but never felt comfortable being on a party’s “team.”
“Once you’re an agent for the team, you’re called upon to answer for the team, even if you disagree with it,” Bengs said.
The Forward Party asks candidates to sign a pledge to support democracy, the constitution and the rule of law, and to support policies to “make elections secure and easy to vote in for all eligible voters, all while striving to represent all of my constituents.”

Former Democratic U.S. presidential candidate Andrew Yang, independent South Dakota U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs and former Republican New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman are pictured on Oct. 25, 2026, at Monks Ale House in Sioux Falls. (Courtesy of Brian Bengs campaign)
 

The pledge says candidates may demonstrate those values by supporting policies that lower barriers for new parties and independents, such as non-partisan primaries and ranked-choice voting, the latter of which allows voters to rank their preferred candidates in order. 
Bengs said he supports all of that and signed the pledge prior to earning the Forward Party’s endorsement. 
“In all seriousness, I would probably not be here in a competitive position today without the support of the Forward Party,” Bengs said. “It’s that type of movement that they’re trying to build, which I’m 100% behind.”
Bengs trailed Rounds by 8 points in an Emerson College/KELO-TV poll released last week. Another poll released last week, from Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy and South Dakota News Watch, showed Rounds ahead 56% to 37%.
The Forward Party has endorsed four U.S. Senate candidates, according to its website: Forward Party candidate Bob Chew in Colorado, and independents Bengs, Seth Bodnar of Montana and Todd Achilles in Idaho, 
After the forum, Bengs told South Dakota Searchlight that he hopes the Forward Party will collect enough signatures to be recognized in South Dakota, which would make it easier for future candidates to run in the state. The party says it’s recognized in Arizona, Utah, Colorado, Minnesota, Florida, South Carolina and Connecticut.
Even without official party status and the resulting ability to nominate candidates, the party’s support meant access to a network of donors for fundraising, Bengs said.
Hopes for victory, Rounds’ response
If any of the Forward Party’s endorsed candidates win, Whitman said, they can have a big impact on the balance of power in a closely divided U.S. Senate by forcing both parties to work with them to earn passage of major legislation. She told the crowd that the Forward Party’s nominees have all pledged to caucus with one another, or to at least avoid caucusing with either major party.
After the forum, Whitman told Searchlight she was in Sioux Falls early and campaigned with Bengs, knocking on “about 100” doors.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
A strong second-place finish in any of the states with a Forward Party-endorsed candidate would send a message to the major parties about the public’s desire for more options, Whitman said, but “I think Brian has a very good chance of winning.”
Bengs said he expects to win the Senate race. When asked what he might see as a positive sign if he doesn’t, though, he said winning 48% of the vote would send a strong message and support the mission of candidates who want to see the two-party system reformed.
“Obviously, I want to get to 51%,” Bengs said, but he added that Nebraska independent Dan Osborn’s 46% against Republican Deb Fischer in that state’s 2024 U.S. Senate race convinced Bengs that he could run as an independent in South Dakota and have a chance.
Osborn is running again in 2026, again as an independent, against Republican U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts.
Rob Skjonsberg, a spokesman for Rounds, said in a text message to Searchlight that Bengs’ support from the Forward Party “makes sense.” Rounds’ campaign ads, as well as previous statements from Skjonsberg, have accused Bengs of being a Democrat at heart, not an independent.
“The Forward Party — which isn’t a party — is a well connected, liberal D.C. outfit that promotes fake independents in red states,” Skjonsberg said. “It’s founded by another fake independent and Democrat candidate that believes in universal income equality.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: At ‘cross-partisan’ town hall, Osborn shares stage with Democrat, ex-Republican and former RNC chair
text:
California Democratic U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, former U.S. Rep. Joe Walsh, former RNC chair Marc Racicot and Dan Osborn during a panel discussion at the University of Nebraska at Omaha on Oct. 24. 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — Registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn held a town hall Saturday with California Democratic U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, former U.S. Rep. Joe Walsh, and former Republican National Committee chair Marc Racicot. 
Nebraska U.S. Senate candidate Osborn and the panel, which was moderated by former Nebraska Libertarian Party chair Rachael Nelson, took questions from the audience on such topics as transgender athletes, government reform, gun control and division in America at an event the Osborn campaign called “cross-partisan.” But incumbent Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts’ campaign questioned how bipartisan it was. 
“I don’t know of many candidates running for office right now who can put a Libertarian, a progressive, a Tea Party guy, a Republican and a bunch of independents in the same room,” Walsh told the audience at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. “That says something.” 
Osborn said he hopes to have discussions that bring people around ideas everyone can agree on. 
Walsh, of Illinois, served one term as a Republican U.S. House member and ran against President Donald Trump in the 2020 Republican primary. He became a Democrat in 2025.
Racicot served as RNC chair in the early 2000s and has been critical of Trump since 2016.
 Khanna is considered a progressive Democrat.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The first question from the audience was whether Osborn would oppose a ballot measure that would constitutionally limit sports participation in public K-12 schools and colleges to teams of biologically male, female or coed students. 
The former labor leader said the ballot measure is about “fear” that is meant to divide people. 
“I just really do truly think that this is all designed to be divisive,” Osborn said. “I’m not playing that because I believe, you know, in the Constitution of the United States, and I believe in the Declaration of Independence. When the words, they say, ‘life, liberty, pursuit of happiness,’ full stop.” 
Khanna, who is considering a 2028 presidential bid, said he is tired of a “Democratic Party that has thrown the trans community under the bus.” 
“We need to stand up for the dignity of every person,” Khanna said. “Come on, give me a break. Have you ever been on a soccer field and seen the trans kid play? You think there’s some star athletes competing for the Olympics? This is the only thing they have for belonging.” 
Nationally, Republicans have used transgender rights as a wedge issue against Democrats, specifically whether trans athletes should be allowed to participate in girls’ sports. Some Democrats running have tried to distance themselves from the issue or called it a distraction. 
The Jeffrey Epstein files were brought up. Khanna said Osborn would “ stand with survivors and stand for justice” because he would support Epstein Files Transparency Act II. 
Khanna helped push a House discharge petition alongside outgoing Kentucky Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie that forced a vote on the U.S. House’s Epstein Files Transparency Act.  The Epstein Files Transparency Act II hasn’t gotten a vote yet, but Massie said it is two signatures short of forcing a floor vote.
Ricketts and Osborn have attacked each other regarding the Epstein sex abuse controversy. Osborn accused Ricketts of “voting against” the release of the Epstein files — but Ricketts did vote with the rest of the state’s federal delegation to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act. 
Ricketts attacked Osborn over a canceled fundraiser with a longtime Democratic donor who was mentioned in an email in the Epstein files. The donor said “nothing pertaining to me in the March 2024 email” was true.
Other questions Saturday focused on regulating AI, reaching people disengaged from politics, and expanding the number of representatives in Congress. 
Racicot said that to “save” democracy, people must keep working to support candidates like Osborn. 
“(Osborn) believes in service to this nation and to the people he lives with, and he will serve not only the United States Congress. … He will also be involved in, I think, influencing the entire planet. So, don’t be afraid of this. It’s unique,” Racicot said. 
The Ricketts campaign released a statement ahead of the event attacking the panel, saying it “completely unmasks Dan Osborn’s fake independent facade.”
Ricketts’ deputy campaign manager Max Oberg said in a statement that the media should ask Osborn if “he agrees with Ro Khanna that we should shut down Nebraska feedlots? And if he doesn’t, why is he campaigning alongside the radical Democrat who wrote legislation doing exactly that? Nebraska farmers and ranchers deserve an answer.” 
Osborn didn’t take questions after the event. The general election is Nov. 3. Early voting has already started.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Trump invokes anti-Muslim rhetoric to attack El-Sayed at Michigan rally supporting Rogers, James
text:
President Donald Trump takes the stage at a rally for U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)PORT HURON — President Donald Trump on Sunday held a rally in Port Huron to energize Michigan Republicans in a bid to elect Mike Rogers to the U.S. Senate and John James as governor, spending a considerable amount of time in his speech attacking Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, launching into anti-Muslim rhetoric against the candidate in a bid to convince his base to show up and defeat him.
“I’m here today to keep a jihadist … Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Trump said at the top of his remarks.
The president’s visit also followed a Saturday rally featuring former President Barack Obama and the Democratic slate up for election in 2026, with a heavy emphasis on boosting the prospects of El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, Michigan’s secretary of state. El-Sayed has been working to shore up the Democratic coalition following struggles with Jewish and Black voters, and Obama’s visit aimed to bridge some of the lingering divisions within the party.
In response to those roadblocks, Rogers has been hammering El-Sayed with campaign stops in Detroit and other places where Democrats typically dominate at the ballot box. 
While Port Huron is not in that category — it sits in a district considered to be the most Republican in the state by the Cook Partisan Voting Index and is represented by conservative stalwart U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) — the area showed visible support for Republicans, with Rogers yard signs lining neighborhoods surrounding its downtown area.
Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers, right, speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump, left, on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Supporters of President Donald Trump attended a rally for U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Michigan Speaker of the House Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) takes the stage at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump for U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Bruce Township) speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump for U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers and gubernatorial candidate John James on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers speaks at a rally hosted by President Donald Trump on Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center in Port Huron, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Still, Trump has been telling crowds of supporters at rallies across the nation that they should vote in November as if he is on the ballot — a theme he invoked again in Michigan this weekend.
Although Trump meandered through an address in which he spoke admiringly about Ohio U.S. Sen. Jon Husted’s physical appearances, complimenting the buttocks of rap artist Nicki Minaj — who was in the audience sitting next to James and Rogers — and about how manly he thought Rogers was, Trump’s main focus was El-Sayed.
“This great state was built by generations of American patriots who shed their blood, sweat, and tears, and even gave their lives to defend American freedom,” Trump said. “Abdul El-Sayed’s entire agenda is to burn that legacy down, and he wants to do that. He’s the face of the modern Democratic Party. If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hoards of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence … We’re not going to let this guy become a senator of the United States.”
Lack of ‘moral outrage’ over Islamophobia is helping normalize religious hate, advocates say

Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both flown in to boost Rogers during the primary season, where he faced no opposition, and into the early days of the general election contest. At each of those rallies, Trump and Vance have attacked El-Sayed specifically by calling him a communist, an ungrateful “weasel” and unloading a barrage of Islamophobic scorn against the progressive U.S. Senate candidate.
Rogers has joined them in deploying anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed by emphasizing his full Arabic name, questioning his loyalty to the U.S. and the Constitution, and by claiming he has ties to terror groups — namely the Muslim Brotherhood. While there is no evidence that any of his immediate family were directly involved in the Muslim Brotherhood or international terror networks, Rogers continues to claim that El-Sayed has received donations from individuals connected to Islamic extremism.
Trump on Sunday continued those attacks, while some of his supporters yelled obscenities about El-Sayed, including calling him a “traitor.”
Trump also spoke directly to Jewish voters, as the state Democratic Party works to retain those voters, saying that “any Jewish person that supports this guy should be ashamed of themselves.”
“You know, I’m polling 99% in Israel, and I cannot understand how anybody who’s Jewish can even think about voting for this guy,” Trump said. “Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane. They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate.”
Trump’s racist ‘Truth Social’ post also included whopper on debunked Michigan election fraud theory

On Rogers, Trump said that the Republican was as American as “apple pie. He’s like perfect.”
“This guy, he’s like Central Casting. He’s what your state is all about. He really is. He’s a fantastic man. He’s going to be one of the great United States senators, Mike Rogers,” Trump said. 
Trump has also focused on Michigan’s handling of elections. His administration deployed federal monitors to Michigan during the August primary after state Republicans requested the U.S. Department Of Justice’s assistance in preventing alleged cheating in favor of Democrats — furthering his repeatedly debunked claims of mass election fraud following his loss in the 2020 election.
Benson was secretary of state for both the 2020 and 2024 elections, the latter of which she won handily in Michigan. Still, Trump’s ire for Benson and the state’s Democratic-led executive branch has made her race against James personal, especially considering that James was leaving Congress to run for governor, a decision that has left his 10th Congressional District seat vulnerable to being flipped by Democratic nominee Christina Hines.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Benson, Trump said Republicans in the audience, including Michigan House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township), needed to keep an eye on her during the election, furthering the unfounded contention that Benson could influence the election because she’s on the ballot this year. 
There have been past examples of past Michigan secretaries of state running for higher office while they held the secretary’s position, namely Republican Ruth Johnson, who is now a current state senator. Additionally, Benson publicly announced firewalls had been created within the Michigan Department of State around the election and has recused herself from making any decisions impacting the gubernatorial contest.
“Will you please watch it, fellas? Especially with Benson, you got to watch it,” Trump said. “Bad things happen with the vote counter, so you have got to be careful. … Benson was a disaster. She cheated more, in my opinion, than anybody else, any other politician in the entire United States. You’ve got to watch all those Detroit votes.”
Trump also called Benson “a thief,” with the president again claiming that the 2020 election was somehow stolen, a lie he continues to tell despite being debunked by Democrats and Republicans alike.
Although the emphasis was on Rogers and El-Sayed, James did get one shoutout from Trump, the president urging his followers to support him if they haven’t already voted early or by absentee ballot.
“You’ve got a very good man, a man who I know so well, and he’s going to be really, I think, a fantastic governor,” Trump said of James.
