name: VTDigger
title: Turning tragedy into baskets: One partnership brings conservation and craft together
text:
Joanne Garton, community forester with the Vermont Urban & Community Forestry Program, in a stand of black ash trees in Hardwick on Sept. 25, 2026. The trees marked with an orange ribbon have been treated with an insecticide, which will help protect it from an emerald ash borer infestation. Photo by Bear Savage/
A slab of bark from a recently-harvested black ash tree covered one of the big picnic tables at Atkins Field in Hardwick in late September, where a basketmaking workshop was unfolding. Emerald ash borer larvae – which look like tiny worm-like creatures, pale white in color with a dark dot for a face – dotted the characteristic swooping S-curve tunnels that scarred the bark.
Those S-curve galleries are a death sentence for many ash trees, but especially black ash trees, a wet soil-loving species that researchers say mount little to no resistance to the threat of the emerald ash borer.
The black ash tree was harvested to support a splint-making workshop series, where participants helped produce splints, which are strips of wood peeled from a black ash log. The workshop was funded primarily through the U.S. Forest Service. It was hosted by the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation and by Kerry and Aaron Wood, who are enrolled citizens of the state-recognized Nulhegan Band of the Coosuk Abenaki Nation.
Kerry Wood said it’s important to think of trees – and the water and the air, among other parts of nature – not as things, but as “someones,” as a brother or sister.
“If we think about the earth as being someone, we might treat them differently than we’re at in this day and age,” she said.
The workshop series allows the public to help create splints that can be stored and potentially used for basketmaking for hundreds of years. The most recent workshop, which took place at Orchard Valley Waldorf School in East Montpelier on Oct. 17, was the final one planned for the year, but the organizers expect the workshops will continue. They hosted five workshops this year, including in Rutland and Chittenden counties.
Basketmaking with black ash trees is a culturally significant practice that has been around for thousands of years. It’s present in Indigenous origin stories and ceremonial practices, as well. Basketmaking is a process with many steps, which starts with harvesting a tree, stripping it of its bark, pounding it to make splints, preparing the splints to be woven, and finally weaving them into baskets.
Robin Wall Kimmerer, a scientist, professor and enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, wrote about basketmaking traditions for Potawatomi people in her New York Times bestseller book “Braiding Sweetgrass.”
“Black ash and basket makers are partners in a symbiosis between harvesters and harvested: ash relies on people as the people rely on ash. Their fates are linked,” she wrote.

The log of a black ash tree, which has been partially pounded by participants at the splint pounding workshop in Hardwick on Sept. 25, 2026. Emerald ash borer larvae created the S-curve galleries on the log. Photo by Bear Savage/VTDigger

The emerald ash borer, a small, metallic-green beetle, arrived in the U.S. from Asia. It’s not certain how it arrived, but researchers believed it could have come on wood packing material like pallets or crates. It was first detected in the Midwest in 2002 and its presence was confirmed in Vermont in 2018. The beetle has been confirmed in every county of the state, mostly recently in Essex County, which was thought to be the final holdout of unaffected ash trees in Vermont.
Experts say almost no black ash trees will survive the spread of emerald ash borer, but there are groups who are working to preserve what’s left and honor the trees that won’t survive.
Joanne Garton, one of the workshop organizers, said the logs for the workshop were harvested from two areas that have been affected by emerald ash borer: one in Hardwick, and another in Green River Reservoir State Park in Hyde Park.
The wood is extremely heavy – it is unique in its ability to hold large amounts of water, thriving best in swampy, wet areas.
Kerry and Aaron Wood both apprenticed for three years under master basketmaker Jeanne Brink, a cultural preservationist who passed away last year. They have since helped lead multiple workshops, including this series of splint-making workshops.
Community forester Garton said it’s unique that the workshops can focus specifically on black ash tree education and outreach.
“We know the clock is ticking with ash and emerald ash borer, so it’s felt very appreciated and timely,” she said. “This type of work, we won’t be doing it forever. Eventually, we (likely) won’t have logs to pound.”
Garton said at the moment, there’s a bottleneck of logs to be pounded, which takes a lot of people power. She said that while managing emerald ash borer-infested trees, which can involve cutting down trees, some land managers are trying to get these felled trees to basketmakers. People with all kinds of interests and backgrounds have been showing up to these workshops, and she said everybody’s contribution weaves together in this collective effort.
“You end up becoming part of the story because you chose to be present in it,” she said.
A couple dozen people showed up to the most recent workshop, despite bitterly cold winds. Even more people attended the previous workshop in Hardwick, and it coincided with the Hardwick Farmers Market. VTDigger attended both. Some attendees had woodworking experience, some were interested in the basketmaking process, some were just coming to learn as much as they could.

Aaron Wood (second from left) and workshop participants pound black ash logs into splints in Hardwick on Sept. 25, 2026. Photo by Bear Savage/VTDigger

One of the workshop leaders, Aaron Wood, explained that the goal when making splints is to pound every square inch of the log with sturdy, even whacks.
He said in each tree ring in the trunk of the black ash, which represents one year of tree growth, there is a distinction between the wood the tree makes throughout that year. The wood a tree makes in the spring is softer, like straws, because it is growing quickly and pulling water and nutrients up through its roots. Pounding crushes the ‘straws’ and leaves behind the ‘late growth,’ which is when tree growth slows down in the summer and into the fall. 
Equipped with the warmth of a small fire, hot cider and a pile of mallets, workshop participants started whacking on the 6- to 8-foot logs, their collective bangs dipping into and out of synchrony.
Then, mallet-wielders tried their hand at peeling the strips of wood, which were pale, a little shaggy and splintered, and curved slightly as they were freed from the log. After a few hours, several dozen splints formed a pile on a moving blanket by the next stage of the process – splitting. Splints can often be peeled even further to make thin, but very strong, “wooden ribbons,” as Kerry Wood described them.
Aaron Wood said that once these logs are processed into splints, they can be preserved for hundreds of years. He said preparing them now can keep the basketmaking tradition alive, even if black ash trees largely disappear from the landscape. He also hopes there might be enough black ash trees protected from the emerald ash borer that people will be able to visit them.
“‘This is our relative. This is one that we have been saving,’” Wood said. He said he hopes to be able to tell people if there are living examples of the tree. He said it’s important to try, “so that people can come and appreciate it and develop that relationship with it.”

Fancy baskets woven by Kerry Wood and displayed at the splint pounding workshop in Hardwick on Sept. 25, 2026. Photo by Bear Savage/VTDigger

Mattison Brady, who helps to monitor a small plot for the progression of emerald ash borer in the area, said he enjoyed learning more about the basketmaking process.
“In the last half hour, I just kind of got the tactile experience of how hard you have to hit a log and what it takes to pull it up…” he said. “Which I didn’t know until this moment. So that’s pretty cool.”
Brady also appreciated the community element of the event.
Garton, the community forester, said there are some efforts underway to slow the spread of emerald ash borer, or EAB. She is a certified pesticide applicator, and administers systemic insecticide, which is injected into the base of the trunk, on a small number of ash trees on state lands. She said the insecticide can be very effective at protecting a tree from an infestation, but it needs to be injected every couple of years. It’s more of a targeted method, and it’s generally not practical or cost effective to treat woodland trees, according to the Urban Forestry Program.
There is also a collective effort among many partner groups, like the Intervale Center and the NorthWoods Stewardship Center, to gather black ash seeds with volunteers and preserve them for the future. Another citizen-science ash monitoring program works to identify ‘lingering trees,’ which are trees that seem to have survived an emerald ash borer infestation that impacted the rest of the ash trees in the area. Saving these seeds are of particular interest, especially if they seem to have resisted the beetle.
“You’re running the clock a little against EAB, and (against) these trees dying,” Garton said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Turning tragedy into baskets: One partnership brings conservation and craft together.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Candidates running as independents don’t always seem, well, independent
text:
Legislators mingle in the South Dakota House of Representatives ahead of the governor's budget address on Dec. 6, 2022, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)As if South Dakota’s two-party system wasn’t weak enough, now there are a slew of independent candidates up and down the ballot. While the number of independents running for the Legislature is unusual, it’s hard to tell just how independent those candidates will be.
South Dakota’s two-party system is weak because candidates from the Democratic Party, more often than not, fail to show up. That’s the case again this year in the Legislature with the Democrats handing majorities to the Republicans in the House and Senate before a single vote is counted.
Democrats’ absence is felt elsewhere on the ballot as Republican Lance Russell faces no opposition for state attorney general. Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds is facing only an independent candidate, Brian Bengs. The candidacy of Bengs has received some national attention as South Dakota is one of four states fielding credible independent candidates for the U.S. Senate.
Unusually high number of independent candidates seek South Dakota legislative seats

On a national level, some pollsters are predicting a blue wave that will give Democrats the majorities in both chambers of Congress. With the president’s approval rating at a new low, that blue wave may lift a few independent candidates as well.
It’s hard to see how that wave gains much momentum further down the ballot in deep red South Dakota. Yet, the Legislature has an unusually large number of independent candidates this year — eight in House races and three in Senate races. In the District 27 House race, an independent is sure to win election as four independents and one Republican are running for two seats. That will be the first independent to win a South Dakota legislative seat since 2010.
The cachet of running as an independent doesn’t stop at the Legislature. In Brookings County, where I live, independent candidates for county finance officer and sheriff are running against Republican candidates. There are five candidates for three openings on the county commission: three are Republicans and the other two are independents.
Voters usually have at least a vague idea of what it means when a candidate is registered as a Republican or a Democrat. A candidate who’s on the ballot as an independent is tougher to figure out. A South Dakota Searchlight story tried to get a sense of the independent candidates seeking election to the Legislature. For some of those candidates, their intentions remain vague.
Neal Tapio of Watertown, who faces two Republican challengers for two House seats, and Joe Flood, who is one of the four independents in District 27, told Searchlight that they always planned to run as independents in this election. Flood said, “I don’t think either party has covered itself in glory.”
Two candidates, District 27 Senate candidate Peri Pourier, and District 27 House candidate Evangeline Poor Bear, missed the filing deadline to run as Republicans and consequently used the later filing deadline for independent candidates to get on the ballot.
Pourier, in particular, is a political chameleon. She was first elected as a Democrat and then switched to the Republican Party. Now she’s running as a calendar-impaired independent.


Let us know what you think...


 

For District 23 independent state Senate candidate Brian Breitling, filing as an independent was a way to avoid a primary with a popular Republican incumbent. As luck would have it, the incumbent, Tom Pischke, withdrew from the race when faced with two felony counts of filing a forged or false instrument for allegedly signing and submitting candidate nominating petitions for county party precinct positions without the candidates’ knowledge.
Now Breitling faces a replacement Republican candidate in the race, but it’s really a distinction without a difference. “I’m a Republican running as an independent,” Breitling told South Dakota Searchlight. “That’s what I tell people when I’m knocking on doors.”
No wonder it’s so tough to figure out what it means when a candidate is running as an independent. The R, D or I after a candidate’s name should be a signal to voters about what the candidate believes. At the very least, when someone is running as an independent it should mean that the candidate has a clear disdain for the two-party system. Running as an independent shouldn’t be an expedited way to get on the ballot to avoid a party primary fight or a loophole used when the filing deadline comes as a surprise.

name: Mississippi Today
title: House speaker’s poll: Mississippians want to eliminate property tax even if it means higher retail costs
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippians seem to be providing contradictory responses to questions asked in a recent poll commissioned by state Republican House Speaker Jason White.
On the one hand, according to the 501 people questioned in the scientific poll, their top priority was inflation or the cost of most retail goods, such as clothes, groceries, gasoline and many other items.
But on the other hand, a majority of those polled say they would favor eliminating the tax on primary residences (or on homesteads) and offset that lost revenue by increasing the sales tax, resulting in those retail items costing more.
Despite those increased costs, 56.6% of poll respondents said they would favor eliminating the property tax on primary residences while increasing the sales tax, while 24.6% opposed the proposal and 18.9% offered no opinion. Inflation was the top priority of 22.2% of respondents, followed by crime and public safety at 19.1% and healthcare at 14.7%. Only 13.5% said reducing taxes was their top priority.
Maybe, the people who identified inflation as the top priority were among the respondents opposed to eliminating the property tax and increasing the sales tax. Maybe, some poll respondents weighed the options and decided they would rather pay no property tax even if it resulted in increased costs for retail items.
No polling explanation offered
The polling firm – Republican-leaning Cygnal – did not attempt to explore that contradiction.
White and his House Republican leadership are currently exploring the option to eliminate the homestead property tax and increase the sales tax.
The option is being considered even though Mississippi has one of the lowest property tax rates in the nation with an effective property tax rate of 0.58% – meaning homeowners on average pay .58% of the value of their home in property taxes.
It should be pointed out that property taxes fund city and county governments and are levied by local officials under the restraints put in place in state law. Property tax rates could be significantly higher in some cities and counties than in others.
Mississippi has a 7% statewide sales tax on most retail items. The sales tax on food recently was reduced to 5%.
Most of the sales tax revenue currently goes to the state, but 18.5% of it is returned to the municipality where the sales tax was collected. Counties currently receive no sales tax revenue.
The sales tax is the largest single source of state revenue, accounting for more than 38% of the general fund used to fund state government services, and it will become even more important thanks to plans to eliminate the income tax. Based on recent legislation, the income tax, which currently accounts for a little less than 28% of the state general fund revenue, will be phased out sometime in the late 2030s.
Sales tax vs. property tax
With Mississippi eliminating the income tax, and already beginning to face budgetary pressures, it will be difficult for the state to provide any money to local governments to offset the potential loss of the homestead property tax. If the Legislature eliminates the property tax, local governments will be dependent on an increase in the sales tax with the revenue going to them. 
The homestead tax generates significantly more than $1 billion annually for cities and counties, according to Jason Camp, an extension specialist with the Center for Government and Community Development at the Mississippi State University’s Extension Service.
According to the Tax Foundation, when combining  funds for both local and state governments, the sales tax accounts for 35.1% of the total revenue while the property tax accounts for 26.4% and the income tax accounts for 16.8%, though that is steadily declining as the income tax is phased out.
The bottom line is that it will take a significant increase in the sales tax to offset the cities’ and counties’ loss of the homestead property  tax revenue. And the result will be Mississippians facing higher prices at retail establishments. How much of an increase is perhaps the key question for House leaders to ascertain before taking any action during the legislative session that begins in January.
Perhaps the question Speaker White should get his pollsters to ask before the 2027 session begins is whether Mississippians want to forgo government services or pay higher prices for retail items or keep paying what is one of the lower homestead property rates in the nation.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Commentary: Arkansas Democrats have their best opening in years. What if they still can’t win?
text:
U.S. Senate candidate for Arkansas, Hallie Shoffner takes the stage on Thursday, October 1, 2026 at the Ballots, Blue Jeans, & BBQ fundraiser in North Little Rock. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Long before it was Trump country, Arkansas was the Democratic holdout among Southern states, a lonely bluish island surrounded by red.
Heading into Election Day, state Democrats may have to grapple with the inverse situation if Arkansas remains solidly red in the middle of what many are predicting could be a blue wave.
State Democrats have been increasingly optimistic about their chances of an upset in a state where they haven’t won statewide or federal office in 16 years. There’s good reason for that.
President Donald Trump’s low approval numbers, an unpopular war in Iran, anti-incumbent sentiment and high prices that have hit the state’s farmers particularly hard have created the best environment for Democrats in Arkansas in years.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
But there are enough warning signs to temper that enthusiasm, and they point to longer term challenges the party will need to address if they can’t capitalize on such a favorable climate.
The latest sign of trouble came from the same pollsters who boosted the party’s hopes just a couple months ago. Polling this month from Talk Business & Politics and Hendrix College showed Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton having a 9 percentage point lead over Democratic challenger Hallie Shoffner in his reelection bid.
The poll, which had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points, was a major swing from Talk Business’ August poll that showed the race statistically tied, with Shoffner holding a lead that was within the margin of error.
The numbers were even starker for the governor’s race, which showed Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders holding a double-digit lead over Democratic challenger state Sen. Fred Love. The poll showed 11% of respondents supporting Libertarian Colt Shelby.
There’s been a dearth of polling in Arkansas, and it’s dangerous to read too much into only two polls. The polling comes as Democrats face a lack of resources and national support that could be the biggest obstacles in the midterms here.
One of the most notable storylines nationally about the midterms is how bullish Democrats have become about their chances in predominantly Republican states where Trump won two years ago. They’ve invested in red states like Kansas, Texas and South Carolina. Even neighboring state campaigns for governor in Oklahoma and the U.S. Senate in Mississippi have received a late infusion of spending from the national party.



Let us know what you think...


 


But Arkansas’ races for Senate and governor appear to be mostly off the national party’s radar. Political forecasters have labeled the race for governor as solidly Republican, and Love has struggled in fundraising.
In the Senate race, Shoffner has received some national attention. But nearly all forecasters have also rated the race in Cotton’s favor. A major exception is the Almanac of American Politics, which recently moved the race to from solid to “likely” Republican.
National Democrats have mostly steered clear of the race, something Shoffner has pointed to as a plus. Her campaign touted how she’s received “zero investment” from the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in a recent release. And when former Vice President Kamala Harris spoke at a state Democratic Party fundraiser earlier this year, Shoffner made a point of keeping her distance from the event.
At the same time, Cotton and Republican groups have been heavily outspending Shoffner. The Republican incumbent lawmaker’s campaign has about $4 million more in the bank than Shoffner. America One, a conservative super PAC, has spent more than $4.4 million on the race so far this year.
The spending comes nowhere close to the more than $50 million that was spent by both sides in 2014, when Cotton unseated then-Democratic Sen. Mark Pryor. But the figures highlight the gap Democrats face in getting their message out to voters, especially with Cotton repeatedly hammering Shoffner over issues like immigration.
The more level playing field could come in Arkansas’ 2nd Congressional District, where Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill is trying to fend off a challenge from Chris Jones.
Jones has had an assist from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee as well as from national Democratic figures like Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has put more than $1 million into the race. Hill has also had outside help, with two cryptocurrency-focused PACs spending on the race. 
It’s not the first time both national parties have spent heavily on the race. But the environment could be more difficult after 2021’s redistricting made the 2nd District more favorable to Republicans by carving out sections of Little Rock.
Despite the challenges, there’s still room for hope for Democrats. The first day of early voting in heavily Democratic Pulaski County far outpaced first day numbers in the past two midterm elections. And how aggressively Cotton and Hill are blanketing the airwaves with ads speaks as loudly as any polls about how competitive they view their races.
The pivotal question for Democrats after the votes are tallied on Nov. 3 may not be who ultimately wins, but whether the party creates something durable that gives them a shot in a post-Trump era.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Across Connecticut, anxiety fuels data center backlash
text:
Local officials in many parts of Connecticut are not waiting for the national data center boom to come to them.
Earlier this month, for example, the East Lyme Zoning Commission voted unanimously to adopt an indefinite ban on all data center development, one of the first such blanket prohibitions in Connecticut. The ban, which goes into effect on Saturday, came before anyone had announced even the faintest plan to construct a data center in the coastal town.
“It seems like all over the country, they’re trying to figure out the effects of pollution, energy consumption, chemical runoffs,” Anne Thurlow, the chairwoman of East Lyme’s Zoning Commission, said during an August meeting.
“I think it’s a good thing to ban them until we know more about them,” Thurlow added. “It could always be reversed if the town wanted to.”
East Lyme is one of around half a dozen municipalities that have taken preemptive action to block data center development, either through temporary moratoriums or a complete ban, according to a review of public meetings and records by the Connecticut Mirror.
Moratoriums have been passed in communities big and small, suburban and rural. New Haven passed a one-year moratorium in September, with an exemption for the city’s existing quantum computing hub. Morris, a town in the Litchfield Hills with fewer than 3,000 residents, has a two-year ban.
“The Connecticut case is quite interesting because many other places in the country, when we see these protests and opposition, either something has started or something is already there,” said Subodha Kumar, a professor statistics, operations and data science at Temple University’s Fox School of Business.
But in Connecticut, he said, political pushback has formed well ahead of actual plans for development.
“Connecticut has never been that attractive, frankly speaking, for data centers,” Kumar said.
The development of large “hyperscale” data centers in Connecticut, and to a greater extent in New England, has been stymied by the high cost of electricity, along with the need to access to utility infrastructure and large plots of land to house thousands of servers, which can easily cover several football fields.
In 2021, Connecticut lawmakers fast-tracked legislation to lure data center developers by promising to waive sales and use taxes for projects that invest at least $200 million in the state (or $50 million for projects located within certain state-designated enterprise zones). To date, the only project to take advantage of that exemption: Cigna’s $386 million renovation of an existing data center in Windsor.
Thurlow said that the effort in East Lyme was driven, in part, as a reaction to a proposal to erect a massive new data center facility next door in Waterford, which is home to the Millstone Nuclear Power Station. The planned facility would have drawn its power directly from Millstone, a setup known as co-location.
But local pushback and years of delays ended up killing that project, according to Waterford First Selectman Robert Brule, who told the Connecticut Mirror last month that he and the town were no longer interested in hosting data centers.
“We’d rather produce the energy now than produce a project that sucks up the energy,” Brule said.
The Department of Economic and Community Development, which oversees the data center tax incentive program, said it has reviewed only two applications under the program since it began and none this year. The credit has become an issue in the gubernatorial election, with Republican candidate Sen. Ryan Fazio arguing that the tax incentive should be ended.
A spokesperson for Gov. Ned Lamont said that the governor was open to discussing changing or eliminating the credit, adding that the tax incentive was never intended for large AI data centers and “should be clarified to ensure it is never used by a hyperscale data center and that data centers bring their own power.”
The law also exempted qualified projects from local property taxes but requires developers to enter into a host fee agreement with any municipality in which a data center is located. 
Randy Collins, a lobbyist at the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, said developers argued that it would be “economically unfeasible” to invest millions of dollars into the necessary equipment for data centers without offsetting some of the taxes.
But despite a handful of towns successfully negotiating host fee agreements, Collins said developers have been slow to actually take advantage of the tax breaks.
“If you look at the resources and requirements going in, they’re not just going to be popping up everywhere,” Collins said.
Still, the issue has drawn considerable attention. Democrats in the state Senate say the moment requires new policy, with Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff announcing this week that he intends to introduce legislation next session that would create a statewide moratorium on new data centers. The proposal was initially outlined in a CT Mirror op-ed in September.
“We think there should be rules of the road. We think there should be a moratorium,”  Duff told reporters during a Thursday morning press conference in Groton. “We think we should better understand what electric and water and other types of problems are.” 

Mystic resident Paula MacDougall, who lives near a former proposed data center site, speaks with reporters about the importance of a data center moratorium during a press conference on Oct. 22, 2026. At left is Joe de la Cruz, a Democratic candidate for state Senate in the 18th District. At right is Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk. Credit: P.R. Lockhart / CT Mirror

The public concern around data centers, he added, is something worth listening to. “We’re seeing people across our state and across our country who are really upset over the proliferation of data centers coming in, literally in people’s neighborhoods,” Duff said. “We should not have these in people’s neighborhoods.” 
Duff argued that there is a clear partisan divide over data centers. Senate Minority Leader Stephen Harding, R-Brookfield, challenged that assertion, saying that he also would support some sort of pause on data center development and would support repealing the 2021 tax incentive for data centers.
“Clearly, there’s a lot of questions that are unanswered regarding data centers,” Harding said in a brief interview on Friday. “I don’t think we should be siting them currently without further information on the energy they’re going to use and how they’re going to impact the communities where they’d ultimately be sited.”
That bipartisan agreement is perhaps a sign of how quickly public sentiment toward data centers has turned negative, a trend that is unfolding nationally. So far, public backlash to the mere mention of prospective data centers has been swift, vastly outpacing actual construction or even applications.
In interviews with the Connecticut Mirror, state residents said that even if a large number of data centers is unlikely to emerge, communities cannot afford to wait for more projects to be introduced. And they argue that their concerns about the potential impacts of data centers, no matter the size, should be taken seriously. 
Developers, meanwhile, counter that their projects, many of which are less than 40,000 square feet, are being unfairly lumped in with larger data centers, arguing that the facilities they intend to build will have minimal environmental impact and, in some cases, will support the redevelopment of formerly blighted properties and previously contaminated sites. 
Collins said that while the CCM has not taken a formal stance on the issue of data centers, the group generally favors more local control.
The tension is fueling intense debate in communities, not only about data centers but about the pace of technological growth, the advent of artificial intelligence technology and the role communities should play in economic development.
And in some places, the backlash against data centers has followed realistic plans for development.

Anti-data center demonstrators protest at the Pennsylvania state Capitol, Oct. 6, 2026, in Harrisburg, Pa. , File) Credit: AP Photo/Marc Levy

Cromwell
One of the fiercest debates over the construction of data centers is taking place in Cromwell, where energy developer Global Common has publicized plans to construct a 300-megawatt facility, about 550,000 square feet, on land currently occupied by agricultural fields and a former gravel distributor.
Bob Foxen, the chief executive of Global Common, said the site was chosen to take advantage of a buried gas transmission pipeline to power fuel cells that he said will provide all of the electricity to run the data center. He said the size of the property, more than 150 acres, would also allow for setbacks to alleviate visual and noise issues, and to preserve some land for farming.
“I’ve seen the pictures of some data centers, and I think maybe some of them don’t look very pretty,” Foxen said. “But I think ours, you really are not going to see much of anything from the road.”
But before Global Common filed formal site plans with town officials, opposition erupted from residents who said the project was out of scale with the surrounding neighborhood of mostly single-family homes. Social media posts accused officials of having secretly agreed to “fast track” the project, and an online petition against the development drew more than 1,500 signatures.
Cromwell Town Manager Anthony Salvatore said in an interview this week that he’d been introduced to Foxen on one occasion following a meeting with the town’s economic development coordinator.
“The bottom line is, I really don’t have enough info regarding them, and it would not be my approval they need, it’s planning and zoning,” Salvatore said.
In September, the Cromwell Planning and Zoning Commission considered and ultimately rejected a proposed one-year moratorium on data centers.

Developers are exploring a data center project near Watrous Park in Cromwell. Credit: Erica E. Phillips / CT Mirror

One of the residents who spoke up against the idea of a moratorium at that meeting, Allan Wilson, said that some of his initial concerns about data centers had been mollified by researching the ways in which developers can limit water usage and air pollution, including through the use of fuel cells. He said town officials should have the discretion to approve individual projects in the future, if they take appropriate steps to limit negative impacts in the town.
But Wilson added that he remained opposed to specific project being proposed by Global Common just down the street from his home, close enough that he is worried about the potential noise.
“The only benefit to the town is taxes. It’s not like a store you can get anything at,” Wilson said.
While Foxen declined to provide specific figures, he said that any host-fee agreement with the town would provide “millions” in annual revenues and would likely make the data center Cromwell’s biggest taxpayer. He also sought to address residents’ broader anxiety over artificial intelligence and its impact on society.
“I don’t know enough to know if data centers are going to cause the end of the world. That’s beyond my knowledge,” Foxen said, adding that the U.S. faces global competition from countries such as China in the race to develop AI.
“Even if we ban data centers, our adversaries are not going to ban them,” he added. “So there’s that side, and I think they need to be designed in a way that is consistent with the local community and local needs.”
Colchester
In the days before the Colchester Planning and Zoning Commission held its regularly scheduled meeting on Oct. 21, rumors swirled online that the meeting would focus on approving two data centers proposed for Old Amston Road, a remediated brownfield that once served as an auto parts salvage site. 
Residents were encouraged to show up in force to let the city know that a data center was not wanted. 
Liv Pike was one of the residents who answered that call. 
Pike lives on the road where the proposed data centers could be placed. She cares deeply about the environment and believes that a data center, and the artificial intelligence technology that it could support, would create new harms. 
And the research she’s been doing in recent days has only added to her fears. 
“I found out that most of the water that is used to cool down these AI data centers we cannot reuse because they have salt and other chemicals in it. It doesn’t go back into the river system,” she said. “If we did that, we are bringing not just Connecticut and Colchester — we are bringing the world closer to ending, in my opinion.” 
Other residents came prepared to speak too, citing worries about noise and quality of life. Some said that a local moratorium on data centers is needed. 
But when the meeting began on Wednesday evening, members of the commission were quick to emphasize that the project is nowhere near that far along. An application for the facilities, the first step before any further planning, zone change, or public hearing discussions are held, has yet to be filed. 
Colchester First Selectman Bernie Dennler says that the project currently raising concern has been around for years, and predates his time in office. “It’s important for people to understand this is not a Town project,” Dennler said in an email. “Private applicants have the right to submit their proposals to the town, but the town is not a party to this private proposal.”
Should an actual application be filed in the future, “both the applicant and residents have a right to be heard in the process,” he added. 
John Matheson, the CEO of ReNew Developers, a real estate firm that lists the two Colchester sites and a third property in Bristol as “available listings” on its website, says that the public outcry over the project has misconstrued the role his company is playing in the development process. ReNew, he says, is only responsible as a power provider for the properties, adding that they are owned by other parties and that his company would not actually be involved in any construction of a data center. 
Beyond that, Matheson argues that the projects he is involved in differ greatly from the sorts of hyperscale data centers that have drawn national backlash. 
“They’re the size of a garden variety Tractor Supply building, or even a CVS,” he said, noting that the owners intend to operate the sites in ways that are environmentally safe. “These are not big, large, impactful buildings that are being suggested.” 
Bristol
In Bristol, a long-simmering proposal for a facility on Riverside Avenue has rankled local residents, with tensions reigniting this spring. The proposal, which like the proposal in Colchester, counts ReNew Developers as a power provider, faced public backlash as residents raised concerns about its construction in the city, citing concerns about its placement so close to the Pequabuck River. 
The backlash grew so intense that Bristol’s Mayor released a statement that aimed to clear up public perceptions of the project. In the statement, Mayor Ellen Zoppo-Sassu explained what administrative steps the project had already cleared, while also aiming to describe what the proposed facility would do. 
The proposed center, she said, is far different from a hyperscale data center, instead referring to the project as a “micro-cloud building” designed to do something different than an AI-supporting data center. 
“Smaller data centers that bring their own power can be designed for greater sustainability, resulting in a lesser environmental impact and serving as a productive building within the community, which is a goal in Bristol,” she wrote. 
The building, she added, would use less water than local grocery stores or high schools. 
Still, the backlash has been intense, prompting Zoppo-Sassu to support changing local zoning ordinances to prevent the construction of large data centers in the future. 
Beacon Falls
As in other communities, local officials in Beacon Falls — an old manufacturing center along the Naugatuck River — say that the furor over a proposed 100-megawatt data center has gotten ahead of reality.  
“There is absolutely nothing pending, in conversation, on the table, nothing at all for Beacon Falls,” Beacon Falls First Selectman Gerry Smith said in a recent interview. 
The confusion, Smith said, stems from a four-year-old memorandum of understanding between the town and a local developer, O&G Industries, to facilitate the construction of a smaller 32-megawatt data center on a former gravel quarry adjacent to Route 8. Under the terms of that agreement, the data center owners would have paid $2.5 million a year in taxes, with annual increases for inflation. 
That additional revenue would have allowed the town to reduce its tax rate on other properties by more than 13%, according to a copy of the agreement shared with the Connecticut Mirror.
In the end, the project never came to fruition because the developers were unable to find a buyer for the project, Smith said. The tax agreement expired in 2023, before the town could formalize a host fee agreement. 
Smith said he last heard from O&G Industries over the summer, when they reached out to ask whether the town would be willing to entertain a second agreement over a revised proposal. Smith said he responded that he was open to the idea but has yet to hear back with any specific plans. 
“The last time they had serious conversations was four years ago,” Smith said. 
In the meantime, marketing materials published online by a New York real estate firm, the Agency, have begun advertising the O&G project as an upgraded 100-megawatt facility, about 294,000 square feet, powered by on-site fuel cells. 
“The development is designed to accommodate the rapidly evolving requirements of artificial intelligence, machine learning, GPU-intensive computing, cloud infrastructure, and enterprise digital workloads,” a website for the project states. 
Representatives from O&G Industries and The Agency could not be reached for comment this week. 
During a Beacon Falls Planning and Zoning meeting held in August, about a dozen residents showed up to raise concerns about data centers and call for a moratorium, according to minutes of the meeting.
In an interview, Smith expressed frustration at both the protests and the developers, who he said had failed to be proactive in their outreach with the town. And while he said he still sees potential benefits in data center development, he added that obstacles may outweigh any incentives. 
“I was told Connecticut wanted to be the data center capital of the world because all these lucrative developers were moving south and west,” Smith said. “It sounded fantastic — but the cost of doing business in the state of Connecticut is still high. Even if you waive all the taxes, it’s still too expensive.”
Editor’s note: Artificial intelligence was used in the process of researching this story. CT Mirror reporter Angela Eichhorst contributed to this story.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: PAID POST: Can AI tell America’s stories? Join the conversation at Hartford’s Mark Twain House
text:
A two-day celebration honors author Lydia Millet and brings writers, critics, and scholars together to explore creativity in the age of AI.
At a house on Farmington Avenue in Hartford, one of America’s most recognizable literary voices helped change the way a nation told its stories. More than a century later, that same house is asking a new question: What happens to the American voice when machines can write, too?
The Mark Twain House & Museum Credit: The Mark Twain House & Museum
For Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain, storytelling was never simply a matter of putting words on a page. His fiction captured the contradictions of American life, challenged comfortable assumptions, and gave readers characters whose voices felt unmistakably their own. His Hartford home, where he lived with his family from 1874 to 1891, remains a place to encounter the power of those words.
This November, The Mark Twain House & Museum will bring that legacy into the present with a two-day celebration of literature, imagination, and the questions confronting writers today. On Friday, November 6, the Museum will honor Lydia Millet with the 2026 Mark Twain American Voice in Literature Award. On Saturday, November 7, it will welcome authors, editors, critics, educators, and scholars for Creative Writing in the Age of AI, a public symposium examining the future of human creativity.
An American voice for our own time
Now in its tenth year, the Mark Twain American Voice in Literature Award recognizes fiction that speaks to American experiences in a distinctive voice. Established through the support of bestselling novelist and Museum board member David Baldacci and his wife, Michelle, the award includes a $25,000 prize. Its purpose is not to find the next Mark Twain, but to recognize writers who continue his tradition of seeing the country clearly, questioning its conventions, and giving memorable expression to its people.
This year’s recipient, Lydia Millet, is being honored for Atavists, a collection of interconnected short stories published by W. W. Norton & Company. With wit, insight, and compassion, the stories move among families, neighbors, and strangers navigating contemporary American life. Their relationships unfold amid digital distractions, shifting expectations, and a sense of uncertainty about the world around them.
Lydia Millet Credit: Lucas Foglia
Millet, whose work has previously been recognized with finalist honors for both the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award, joins a distinguished group of past recipients, including Ocean Vuong, Jesmyn Ward, Alice McDermott, and Ben Shattuck. The November 6 celebration offers readers an opportunity to gather in Hartford, honor a living writer, and consider why individual voices still matter.
What does creativity mean in the age of AI?
The following day turns from celebrating an exceptional literary voice to examining the forces that may reshape how voices are created, shared, taught, and valued. Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of producing polished prose, summarizing books, and imitating familiar styles. Those capabilities can be useful. They also raise fundamental questions about authorship, originality, copyright, education, and the livelihoods of people who work with words.
Who should decide how creative work is used to train AI systems? What happens when readers cannot easily distinguish machine-generated material from human writing? How should schools help students develop their own voices when a draft can appear at the push of a button? And beyond questions of convenience or efficiency, what do people actually value about a story written by another human being?
On November 7, Creative Writing in the Age of AI will address those questions through a series of conversations designed for anyone who reads, writes, teaches, or cares about the future of the written word. The symposium runs from 9:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. at The Mark Twain House & Museum, with both in-person attendance and livestream registration available.
The day’s discussions will explore the legal and ethical frameworks surrounding AI; the experiences of authors, editors, and publishers; and the changes already reaching classrooms, libraries, and reading habits. A concluding conversation will ask participants to look ahead: What now, and what next?
The lineup includes David Baldacci and Lydia Millet, along with former Washington Post book critic Ron Charles, Asimov’s Science Fiction editor Emily Hockaday, writer and editor Jane Rosenzweig, Twain scholar Matt Seybold, and academics working at the intersections of philosophy, law, and technology. Writer and speaker John Warner will moderate the symposium.
David Baldacci Credit: John Groo
These are not abstract questions reserved for the technology industry. They concern students learning to think on the page, educators deciding what and how to teach, authors trying to make a living, and readers searching for work that moves them.
A historic house, a living conversation
There is a particular resonance to having these conversations in Hartford. During Twain’s years here, American life was being transformed by new technologies, industries, and ideas. He wrote about his society with a combination of curiosity, humor, and skepticism that still feels timely. The home that witnessed the creation of some of his best-known books now offers a setting to ask what the next generation of American literature might become.
The Museum’s role is not simply to preserve the rooms where Twain lived. It is also to keep alive the conversations his work began: about who gets heard, whose stories are told, and what literature can reveal about our shared lives. The November 6–7 weekend is an invitation to take part in those conversations rather than watch them from a distance.
Tickets for the November 6 award celebration are available, and the November 7 symposium offers in-person and livestream options. Discounted in-person symposium admission is available for students and educators; in-person registration includes lunch and refreshments. Whether attending for a favorite author, a professional interest in AI, or a curiosity about where storytelling is headed, visitors will find a timely reason to return to Mark Twain’s Hartford home.
Explore the schedule, speakers, and registration options at marktwainaward.org/2026-avl-weekend.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: In 1927, a farmer was the victim of a Kansas haunting. But was it real?
text:
An abandoned farmstead creaks near Marquette, Kansas, in October 2023. A local and somewhat spooky landmark, the structure blew down in a storm in March 2026. (Photo by Max McCoy / Kansas Reflector)This is my favorite time of year.
It’s not a date but a feeling. It comes after the first frost but before the first snow, when the wind whispers through the falling leaves and the moon hangs like a lantern over the Kansas prairie. This is the season of my birth, and I still carry a childish affection for it. Bring on the candy corn, jack-o-lanterns and, of course, the ghost stories.
Let me share with you now a Kansas ghost story from 99 years ago, a tale that begins like a Washington Irving story but which ends like Greek tragedy. It is a true story, or at least the reporting around it was true enough, although I cannot vouch for the phantom at its heart.
The year is 1927, and the location is a farmstead eight miles northeast of Ellinwood, in Barton County in central Kansas. Located in the fertile Arkansas River Valley, the farm is a prosperous one, and the two-story house there is occupied by 42-year-old A.F. “Fred” Koett, his wife, Ella Mae, and their infant son.
Ella Mae Koett was 15 when they wed.
In newspaper interviews, Fred Koett couldn’t quite get her age correct, always adding a few years, perhaps to make the marriage seem less scandalous. Some accounts report Ella’s age as 21. But in census and other official records, she clearly was 15.
Her maiden name was Waddell, and she was part of a family of laborers brought up from Fort Smith, Arkansas, to work on the Koett place. It was Ella Mae’s job to prepare the meals. The newspapers of the day are silent about how it was that Ella Mae graduated from cook to the second Mrs. Koett, but the Kansas City Star noted that Fred’s family strenuously objected to the marriage. Koett’s father, who owned the farm and several hundred other acres to boot, all but wrote him out of the will.
Fred Koett would inherent lifetime use of the land, but upon his death the farm would pass to the children of his first wife, Mary, who died in 1922. The children were being raised by their aunts and uncles.
How did Mary die? I’m not sure, but there appears no hint in the newspapers of anything but a natural, if tragic, death. The marriage may have been a happy one, at least for Fred, because the local paper in 1916 noted that in the same week Fred became the proud owner of a new Chevrolet automobile — and father to a newborn son.
By 1927, however, Fred’s life revolved around Ella Mae and her family.
Ella Mae was still a teenager of 17, and she had given Fred a new son named Louis Joseph. She had also moved her mother, Sarah Waddell, into the household, along with a brother and his wife.
The trouble began on Decoration Day — now observed as Memorial Day —when the family went on a trip to Otis in Rush County and returned to find that pictures in their Ellinwood home were turned to the wall, even though the house had been locked.
What followed was a series of frightening incidents, strange thumps in the night, ghostly footsteps, and a Bible and a statue of the Virgin Mary being moved. Chairs were tipped over, and food disappeared from the table. Then came sightings of the apparition itself.
Ella Mae said she saw it breeze through a window one night.
Her mother said she saw it “in the form of a woman carrying three candles with green, red, and yellow flames,” reported the Wichita Eagle in 1927. Sarah Waddell said it was just like the apparitions she had seen as a child, foretelling a death unless the family moved.
To others, the apparition was not a woman, but a man.
The Waddell family told Fred Koett it was the ghost of his father, who wanted him to move out.
Whatever it was, the thing made a racket in a clothes closet, and when a hired man went to investigate, it burst out and punched him in the face. The dark man was seen peering into windows but left no footprints in the snow outside. It haunted the farmyard and once stabbed a dog with a pitchfork.
When Fred Koett had had enough, he told reporters, he and some neighbors armed themselves and waited outside for the phantom to appear.
“Tuesday night five of us, myself included, armed with shotguns and pistols, lay in ambush in the farm yard,” the Associated Press reported Koett saying. “About midnight a wraith-like form appeared, soundless and about waist-high off the ground. We let go with everything we had. If it had been human, it would have been riddled with bullets. Instead, it hurriedly departed, sailing over the fence with ease.”
The Associated Press turned lyrical in describing the encounter, saying the phantom “floated soundlessly over a 6-foot wire fence like a slow-motion picture of a pole vault.”
Not to be outdone, the Hutchinson News gave an inspired description of the specter.
“Seven reliable people have seen the ghost and all of them claim he is tall and gaunt,” reported the News, “and when he runs (he makes) a hissing sound, and runs with long jumps, generally landing on his toes.”
A committee of neighbors had been formed to deal with the ghost.
“I believe the fellow wants me to leave,” Koett said, according to the Hutchinson paper. “He’s got something on his mind and maybe that’s it. He wouldn’t keep up his pestering of me if it wasn’t. He hangs pictures backwards, blacked my hired man’s eye, opened the family Bible, changed the statue of the Virgin Mary. Last winter we all saw him peering in windows, but (when) we went outside found no traces in the snow.”
Widely reported in newspapers, the Kansas haunting caught the attention of Charles Fort, the pioneering researcher of anomalous phenomena.
“For months this house had been bewitched” by “an invisible,” Fort wrote in his 1933 book, “Wild Talents.”
He labeled the Ellinwood case as an example of poltergeist activity.
“My general expression is against the existence of poltergeists as spirits — but that the doings are the phenomena of undeveloped magicians, mostly youngsters, who have no awareness of their powers as their own,” Fort wrote.
Modern paranormal investigators might agree with Fort, that the incidents at the Koett farm began with the type of object manipulation associated with poltergeists, those “noisy ghosts” often linked with adolescent girls.
But Fred Koett wasn’t looking for a paranormal explanation.
Instead, he asked the Barton County attorney for protection.
The prosecutor, Wayne Lameroux, seemed amused by the plea.
“Go bring in your ghost and I’ll throw him in jail while I look up the law,” he was quoted as saying by the Associated Press. “We might charge him with disturbing the peace.”
The local sheriff’s department guarded the farm for three nights, but failed to note any unusual activity outside, although there were the usual weird sounds and turned pictures inside the house.
“It’s a real, sure-enough ghost, all right,” Koett said, according to an account in the San Antonio Light newspaper. “But it’s the most ornery, contemptible, indestructible ghost, and it won’t fight fair.”
While most newspapers treated the Kansas ghost story as entertainment, the Kansas City Star was having little of it. The Star was skeptical that anything supernatural was afoot.
“In the first place the ghost at the Koett farm is the crudest that ever was pictured in song or story,” the Star observed early in August 1927. “It does nothing particularly startling and makes its appearances in the form of a human being dressed in dark clothing. All very prosaic, but convincing to Fred Koett, and as it is his ghost probably no one else should complain.”
The primary witnesses to the apparition were all members of the Waddell family, the Star noted.
“Mrs. Koett has given birth to one child and is an expectant mother but she does not let the apparitions frighten her,” the Star reported. “She laughs and jokes about them except when talking before Koett; she says it would not be right to joke about it then because they worry him so much.”
Whether the ghost was real or imagined, Fred Koett gave up.
On a Tuesday in August, he sold all of his personal property at auction and rented the farm to a neighbor. He told reporters that he was going to head for either Oklahoma or Arkansas.
“I couldn’t stand it any longer,” Koett said. “I don’t know what it is that has caused so many mysterious happenings but I’ve experienced things that are hardly believable and I have withstood it longer than any other man would.”
The Koetts landed in Fort Smith, the Waddell hometown.
In 1932, Louis Joseph Koett — an infant when the supposed hauntings occurred in Kansas — fell ill. Not knowing the location of his father, a plea went out over radio station KFPW in Fort Smith: “Persons knowing the whereabouts of A.F. Koett, 22 North Twelfth Street, Fort Smith, notify him that his small son, Louis, 6 years old, is dying.”
Koett was in Ellinwood, and a friend alerted him to the broadcast. He apparently made it back in time to be with the child when he died. The death certificate listed the cause of death as meningitis.
A year later, Ella Mae sued for divorce, claiming “cruel and inhuman treatment,” according to the court record.
In March 1933, the Hutchinson News reported that a farmer by the name of Bob Rick discovered $5,220 in gold coins uncovered by hens pecking at worms in the dirt floor of an implement shed. Rick said the gold had been buried by his late father, who could not remember where the treasure was buried before his death at the age of 84.
Rick had worked the nearby Koett land after the ghost affair.
“It is thought now that someone suspecting that gold or valuables had been buried there terrorized the Koetts in order to drive them away so they could seek the hidden gold,” the Hutchinson paper speculated, but they had the wrong place.
Perhaps a better reason for the “discovery” of the treasure was an executive order by Franklin D. Roosevelt banning most private ownership of gold as of April 5, 1933. Rick conveniently found the gold the month before the deadline and dutifully exchanged it for paper money at a bank at Great Bend, where it was transferred to the Federal Reserve.
Whatever the real story, I’ll bet the chickens didn’t peck up that gold.
I don’t know the details of what happened to the Koetts after the divorce, except that Fred remarried and was living in Muldrow, Oklahoma — not far from Fort Smith — when he registered for the draft in World War II. He appears to have died in 1950, at the age of 65. Also, Ella Mae died in California in 1965, according to the California death index. She was in her 50s.
If I weren’t under deadline pressure for a Halloween column, I’m sure research would turn up more about the Koetts. Or rather my wife, Kim, would turn up more details. She’s an expert researcher who found the death certificate and some of the other official records cited earlier.
Was the Kansas ghost story real?
Fred Koett thought it was real.
But the most disturbing part of the tale is not the phantom that was impervious to bullets, but the legacy of human folly. What frightens us when the wind stirs over the prairie on autumn nights is not what’s out there, but what’s inside of us. Ghost stories are about the dark desires that we the living grapple with, and which happily most of us overcome. The Ellinwood haunting is a study in lust, greed and suspicion.
Happy Halloween.
Max McCoy is an award-winning author and journalist. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Coffee, tea or turbulence?
text:
Just when you thought flying couldn’t get any more unpleasant, our atmosphere has joined the airlines in trying to shake you down.
Consider last week when a flight to Los Angeles suffered a 3,675-foot drop in one minute, leaving passengers screaming and at least one flight attendant bloodied.  Four flight attendants were injured, one was hospitalized, but no passengers were hurt, presumably belted into their seats.



The flight was already descending through 25,000 feet to land and one pilot said he thought it felt like wake turbulence from another jet, even though flight-tracking data reportedly showed no other plane nearby.  But the terror in the cabin was just as real.
Adding literal insult to injury, the flight had to wait at least 30 minutes after landing to park at a gate, even with the injured on board.  Welcome to LAX.
Researchers say that wind shear at jetliners’ cruising altitude, the main cause of clear-air turbulence (CAT), is up 15% since 1979.  Over the North Atlantic, en route to Europe, the number of hours of severe turbulence is up 55%.
What’s causing this increase?  Long term, global warming. This winter there’s a near-record El Niño in the Pacific, which research links to 50% more turbulence over large parts of the U.S. and the North Atlantic.
Professor Paul Williams at the University of Reading in the UK says his models show a doubling or tripling of such turbulence in the coming decades, aviation’s sequel to the increasingly severe storms we’ve experienced lately in the Northeast.
Jetliners’ weather radar can’t see clear-air turbulence. Lidar, the fix that’s been ‘just around the corner’ for decades, is still around the corner.  Commuters on Metro-North are familiar with that kind of unkept promise.
Except in very rare circumstances, turbulence doesn’t cause planes to crash.  In testing, Boeing bent the 777’s wings to 154% of their design limit before they snapped, the wingtips flexing some 24 feet upward.
Turbulence’s greatest danger is tossing those onboard (who aren’t belted) up to the ceiling and back down.  According to the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) flight attendants are 24 times more likely to be seriously injured than passengers.
At one Delta regional carrier, the flight attendants union says crews keep working the aisle through turbulence because they’re graded on passenger satisfaction surveys.  Nothing says ‘customer first’ like sustaining a broken ankle for a five-star review.
About half of turbulence accidents happen during descent or approach, and 60% below 20,000 feet. That’s when crews are up securing the cabin for landing.  The aft cabin is the danger zone, accounting for more than three-quarters of flight attendant injuries… another reason to fly up front in First Class.
Staffing cuts at the National Weather Service don’t help in predicting rough skies. The NWS lost about 15% of its staff to Trump administration cuts and buyouts. Last year the GAO found only 69 NWS meteorologists working in FAA air traffic centers, against a cap of 81. Officials planned to shrink that to 64.  Turbulence up. Forecasters down.  What could go wrong?
What can you do to stay safe?  Well, aside from seeking alternate transportation, like the train, not much.  Sadly, train service to Europe is pretty weak.
Instead, keep your seat belt fastened at all times. Make visits to the washroom infrequent and quick.  Be sure your bags in the overhead are stowed and the bin doors closed tightly.  And most of all, always follow crew instructions, especially during descent when turbulence hits most often.
